They also based their form of reasoning on both the law of causality and the principle of regularity.

The idea is this: a judgment in the observed case was established because of a particular cause. If the same cause is found in an unseen or unknown case, under conditions similar to those found in the observed and known case, then the same effect follows. The same judgment is therefore applied to the unseen case by analogy with the observed one.

If we know that wine is forbidden because it causes intoxication, then the same cause must apply consistently to every drink that resembles wine in this respect. We should therefore judge every intoxicating drink to be forbidden, because the same cause must produce the same judgment wherever it occurs.
The Muʿtazilites and the Ashʿarites, however, understood the idea of cause in fundamentally different ways.
The Muʿtazilites believed that causes are objective. In other words, causes exist in things themselves without the need for outside intervention.
This view follows from their rationalist doctrine. On the same basis, they argued that reason itself can recognize good and evil: that good things are objectively good and bad things objectively bad.
The Ashʿarites, as we have already seen, denied that causality exists objectively in things and events.

For this reason, when they spoke of a “cause” in reasoning from the seen to the unseen, they used the term figuratively rather than literally. Their idea of cause was idealist and far removed from a materialist concept of causality.
They explained the cause used in this kind of reasoning as something that God had made into a cause. If God had not made it one, it would not have been a cause at all.
At the beginning of this chapter, we tried to identify the period when Arab-Islamic thought first came into real contact with Aristotle’s logic, or with Greek logic more generally.
During the discussion, we found several historical signs suggesting that this contact began in the first century AH—the seventh century CE—during the Umayyad period.
Among these signs were the following:

There was growing intellectual contact between representatives of Arab thought under the Umayyads and members of non-Muslim religious schools in Syria and Mesopotamia. These included Jacobite, Nestorian and Sabian schools, where Aristotelian logic was taught alongside the rest of the Greek philosophical tradition.

We considered it highly unlikely that such broad intellectual contact—especially in religious debate between Christian and Muslim beliefs—could have taken place without Arab thinkers being influenced by logic, particularly since members of these schools used logic themselves when debating Muslims.

Al-Shahrastānī says of early theologians who lived across the first and second centuries AH, such as Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ, that they “read the books of the philosophers” (al-Milal wa-l-Niḥal, vol. 1, p. 58).
Al-Suyūṭī, quoting Ibn Kathīr in Ṣawn al-Manṭiq (p. 12), likewise says:

“The sciences of the ancients entered Muslim lands in the first century AH when the Muslims conquered the lands of non-Arabs. But they did not become widespread among them because the early generations forbade people from entering into them.”
Arab historians used the expression “the sciences of the ancients” to mean the sciences of Greek philosophy, including logic.

Here too, we considered it unlikely that theologians in the first Islamic century could have read philosophical books without encountering logic, or that these sciences could have entered Muslim lands without creating some contact with logic.

Indeed, according to al-Suyūṭī’s own statement, attempts to forbid the study of these sciences could hardly have happened unless they had already spread to some extent and begun to influence Muslims. Otherwise, the authorities would have had little reason to fear that they might weaken accepted Islamic beliefs among educated Muslims.
But if these historical signs show that Arab contact with logic began in the Umayyad period, historians also tell us that works of logic were not translated into Arabic until the Abbasid period.
So how did this contact take place under the Umayyads?
The sources are confused and inconsistent on this question, which makes it difficult to identify exactly when contact with logic began and what form that contact first took.
We therefore asked why the sources are so uncertain.
We rejected De Boer’s explanation that the problem was simply caused by the loss of many translations produced in the eighth century CE (History of Philosophy in Islam, p. 29, Arabic edition).
If loss alone were the explanation, we would still have to explain why every eighth-century translation of logic disappeared while many translations from other fields, including literature, survived.
So the question remains: how did Arab thinkers become familiar with logic during the seventh and eighth centuries?

The development of Arab-Islamic society during these two centuries gives us clear evidence that Arab thought knew some of the main questions and basic rules of Aristotelian logic before the eighth century.

Besides the historical signs already mentioned, we can point to a well-known cultural phenomenon: the new Arab sciences that began developing under the Umayyads were already strongly influenced by logical questions.
Arabic grammar, for example, often based its rules on principles that had an Aristotelian logical character.
This close relationship between grammar and logic later appeared in the difference between two major historical schools: the Basran and Kufan schools.
The Basran school became known for its rational and logical approach, and Basran grammarians were even given the title “the people of logic.”
There is really only one way to explain this.

After the Arab conquests, a wide and deep cultural interaction took place with countries that possessed rich and varied intellectual traditions. In those historical conditions, ideas and forms of knowledge that were still alive and developing in those societies naturally entered the growing Arab culture.
Communication between educated people in the conquered lands and Arab intellectuals was active and relatively easy, while debates over religious beliefs were almost part of everyday life.
This is how Greek logic entered the rapidly developing movement of Arab thought.

Its arrival, together with other sciences and forms of knowledge, helped produce important qualitative changes in Arab intellectual life, both in the kinds of knowledge being developed and in the methods used to develop it.
Because we had described the Basran school of grammar as especially rational and logical in its method, we also needed to explain the social factors behind this historical fact.
We showed that Basra in the Umayyad period had two important features.
First, it contained a dense concentration of social groups divided by class, along with strong political parties opposed to Umayyad rule.
Second, because of these sharp social and political conflicts, Basra was subjected to particularly severe forms of social and political repression.
This encouraged the rise of powerful intellectual currents that expressed these conflicts on the one hand, and an ideological opposition to the thought and ideology of the ruling group on the other.
The rational method became the main form taken by this ideological struggle, while logic provided an organized method for using the ideological weapons directed against the rulers.

In the same discussion, we saw that kalām, which developed step by step during the first and second centuries AH—first through the Qadarites and then through the Muʿtazilites—grew along the path of philosophical thought and made use of its rational instrument: logic.
We then tried to deal with another important question: what role did logic play in the development of Arab thought?

We argued that logic entered Arab intellectual life at a time when Arab thought was beginning to move beyond a simple, direct and spontaneous view of the world toward an increasingly complex, abstract and systematic way of understanding it.
In other words, it was entering the first stages of philosophical awareness.
As this happened, the need for a clear rational method gradually became stronger. Logic was the method that could meet this need.
Arab thinkers used it to develop their knowledge and enrich it through their own experience, while responding to the needs of the new society that had emerged after the conquests.
Many different social forces were developing within this society, especially the productive forces working in agriculture and craft production.

The feudal and commercial relations of the period increasingly required these groups to develop new and relatively advanced techniques. These techniques were needed both to satisfy the growing demand for luxury among the newly developing landed and commercial aristocracies of the Umayyad state, and to develop the productive sectors themselves: agriculture, crafts and trade.
Under the influence of these social conditions, the need matured for the great historical movement of translating philosophical, natural, mathematical and medical sciences into Arabic.
Logic became the method used throughout this movement, which translated almost the entire Aristotelian logical tradition together with its later commentaries.
Older Arab historians, and some modern historians as well, offered subjective idealist explanations for the movement that translated sciences from Syriac, Greek and Persian into Arabic.

In this chapter we presented two examples of these idealist explanations in order to show why they were mistaken and to replace them with what we regard as the real historical-materialist explanation.
At this point we had to ask another question: Was Aristotle’s logic the only method Arab thought adopted?
Our discussion showed that although Aristotle’s logic played a major role in the development of Arab thought, it did not remain completely Aristotelian and unchanged.
It was adapted to the conditions of a new society and a new historical period—one that differed from Aristotle’s society and age both in its social relationships and in the level of human knowledge.
We saw that Aristotle’s logic underwent different kinds of adaptation, reflecting the different intellectual positions that grew out of different social and ideological positions.
At the same time, these adaptations did not alter the most basic general laws or the fundamental structure of the Aristotelian logical system.
Before examining the different positions taken toward Aristotle’s logic in Arab thought, we tried to explain the positive and progressive role that this logic played.

The first sign of this positive role was that Aristotle’s logic gave rationalist thinkers both a theoretical and a practical tool for strengthening the idea that human reason should play a central role in acquiring knowledge.
It also helped them resist attempts to reduce all knowledge to a single source.
This was possible because Aristotle’s logic was not purely formal. It was a broad system that dealt with the laws of thought both in their formal structure and in relation to their content.
Here we referred to Lenin’s comment in his Philosophical Notebooks that Aristotle looked for the ontological content of logical processes.

Aristotle did not reduce logic to a technique for manipulating terms. He analyzed different forms of thought and repeatedly tried to connect those forms with the natural relationships reflected in human thinking.
He also tried to establish principles for advancing toward scientific knowledge.
Because of these strengths, Aristotle’s logic had an important and positive influence on Arab-Islamic thought during its period of growth and development in the eighth, ninth and tenth centuries CE.

Aristotle’s view of the object of knowledge, and of the role played by material objects outside the mind in acquiring knowledge, also contributed significantly to some of the materialist tendencies that appeared in Arab-Islamic thought, especially in philosophy.
These positive features of Aristotle’s thought and logic appear to have played an important role in producing the many different attitudes toward Aristotelian logic.
Those attitudes varied according to different intellectual and ideological currents and different social positions.
In Chapter Seven, we identified three main positions.
First came the position of the conservative tendency that we consistently call “Salafi” in this study.
This tendency opposed Aristotle’s logic and philosophy for both religious and social reasons.
The Ashʿarite theologians represented this position, even though they themselves were armed with the methods of Aristotelian logic.
This campaign against Aristotle’s logic began after the defeat of the Muʿtazilites under the Abbasid caliph al-Mutawakkil in 232 AH/846 CE.
People who studied or taught Aristotle’s logic were persecuted, and some religious scholars even issued rulings saying that Islam prohibited both teaching and studying it.
This tendency also opposed Aristotelian thought, both philosophy and logic, but its opposition took a different form.
Its representatives could not free themselves from the influence of Aristotelian logic and continued to use it in their own works.
But they took only its purely formal side and rejected its content and its positive features.
The most important example was Abū Ḥāmid al-Ghazālī (1059–1111), the leading Ashʿarite scholar and the one who had the widest influence on Muslim religious opinion.

Third came a set of theoretical disagreements with particular parts of Aristotelian logic. These appeared among some schools of Islamic law, some theological schools, and some traditions of Sufi philosophy.
Their disagreements with Aristotle’s logic concerned several specific points.

Some theologians rejected Aristotle’s theory of definition, according to which a complete definition is built from genus and differentia—that is, from the broader class to which something belongs and the feature that distinguishes it—in order to identify its essence.
Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī represents this opposing tendency.
He argues that a definition cannot validly be constructed from genus and differentia.
